intro: When you search for a local mortgage advisor near me, you're likely looking for someone nearby who can help you understand your mortgage options and find a suitable deal. A mortgage adviser can recommend mortgages based on your circumstances and must be regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). We can introduce you to a local mortgage broker who will quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for a local mortgage advisor usually need
need_lead: You want expert mortgage advice from someone in your area who can look at your situation and recommend a suitable mortgage.
needs: You are buying your first home and want to know how much you can borrow and what deposit you need.
You are remortgaging and want to find a better deal than your current lender is offering.
You are self-employed or have irregular income and need help proving your affordability to lenders.
You are moving home and need a mortgage that fits your new property and circumstances.
You want to understand the full cost of a mortgage, including fees and protection, before you commit.
context_heading: What to understand about local mortgage advice
context: Mortgage advice is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Any broker or adviser you use should be authorised, or be an appointed representative of an authorised firm, and you can check this on the FCA register. Advisers typically hold a qualification such as CeMAP.

Brokers must tell you whether they search the whole of the market or a limited panel of lenders, and how they are paid, whether by lender commission, a fee, or both. If something goes wrong, you can complain to the firm and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when enquiring
tell: Whether you are buying, remortgaging, moving home or investing in property.
Your approximate property value and the amount you want to borrow.
Your employment status, for example employed, self-employed or retired, and your income.
Any deposit you have available and where it comes from.
Whether you have any credit issues or past mortgage problems.
Whether you also need protection advice, such as life insurance or income protection.
questions_heading: Questions to ask the mortgage advisor
questions: Are you authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority and can you provide your registration number?
Do you search the whole of the market or a limited panel of lenders?
How are you paid for your services, and will you disclose all fees and commissions in writing?
What qualifications do you hold, such as CeMAP?
Will you also look at my protection needs, such as life insurance or income protection?
What happens if I want to complain about your service?

faqs.q: How do I check that a mortgage advisor is properly authorised?
faqs.a: You can check the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) register to see if a broker or adviser is authorised or an appointed representative of an authorised firm. The FCA regulates mortgage advice, so it's important to verify their status before proceeding.

faqs.q: Will a local mortgage advisor come to my home?
faqs.a: Many mortgage advisors offer home visits, but this varies. When you speak to the advisor, ask whether they can meet you at home or if they work remotely by phone or video call.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a mortgage advisor and a mortgage broker?
faqs.a: The terms are often used interchangeably. A mortgage advisor recommends suitable mortgages, while a broker may also handle the application. Both should be authorised by the FCA and explain whether they search the whole market or a limited panel.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay a fee for mortgage advice?
faqs.a: Some advisors charge a fee, while others are paid by lender commission, or a combination of both. Brokers must tell you how they are paid before you commit, so ask for a clear explanation of any fees.

extra_heading: Getting the most from a local mortgage advisor
extra: Searching for a local mortgage advisor near me often means you'd rather sit down with someone face to face than work entirely online, especially if your situation has a few moving parts such as self-employment, a gifted deposit or a past credit blip. Being nearby can make it easier to drop off paperwork and ask follow-up questions in person, though many advisers also work by phone or video, so it's worth asking how they prefer to meet.

When you compare local advisers, look beyond distance. Ask each one whether they cover the whole market or a limited panel, what qualifications they hold, and how they are paid, because two advisers in the same town can offer quite different levels of choice. A short conversation by phone usually tells you whether their approach suits you before you commit to anything.

Remember that the adviser recommends, but the decision is yours. Take time to read the recommendation and ask them to explain anything unclear, including the total cost of the mortgage and any protection they suggest alongside it. If a deal sounds too good to be true, ask how it works and get the key points in writing.

extra_faqs.q: Is a local mortgage advisor better than one I find online?
extra_faqs.a: Not necessarily. What matters is whether the adviser is authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, searches a suitable range of lenders for your circumstances and explains their fees clearly. Being local can make meetings easier, but it isn't a substitute for checking those points.

extra_faqs.q: Can I use a mortgage advisor outside my area?
extra_faqs.a: Yes. Many advisers work with clients across the UK by phone, email and video call, so distance needn't rule someone out. If meeting in person matters to you, ask upfront whether they can offer that.
